sections.html:
Hubbard County sits in northwestern Minnesota, and Park Rapids is the seat. Lakes and woods dominate, and the cities are Akeley, Laporte, Nevis and Park Rapids. Population was 22,369 in the July 2025 estimate, up 4.8% from 2020. There are 14,900 housing units but only 8,964 households, and the 2020 census counted 39.6% of units as vacant, which tells you a big share of homes here are cabins or second homes. Owner occupancy is 83.1% and the median home value is $282,600.

Because so many properties are seasonal, classification is the first thing to check before listing. A cabin or lake home used part of the year is taxed differently from a primary residence.

Two departments share the job. The Auditor/Treasurer runs tax administration, collects delinquent taxes, publishes the delinquent tax list, and handles forfeitures, repurchases and confessions of judgment. The auditor also holds a seat on the county board of equalization.

The assessor works inside Property Records at the Government Center, 301 Court Ave., Park Rapids, MN 56470, phone 218-732-3552. That office covers valuation and classification, homestead, tax reduction programs and the recording of real estate documents, so one trip can take care of a value question and a deed together.

Under Minnesota Statutes 279.01, a parcel with more than $100 in tax pays in two halves, one before May 16 and one before October 16. At $100 or less, the whole amount is due with the first half. Mail counts as on time if postmarked by the deadline, and the treasurer has to waive the penalty one time if the postmark is a single business day late.

Agricultural homestead and qualifying farm land may pay the second half through November 15 with no penalty. Seasonal residential recreational property that is not used commercially, which the statute calls class 4c, is charged the lower homestead penalty rates.

The county has posted a homestead notice for the 2026 assessment. Someone who bought or moved into a home in the past year must apply by December 31, 2026 for the benefit to reach taxes payable in 2027, and the applicant needs to have owned and lived in the home by that date. A relative living there also qualifies. For residential and agricultural property, that means the owner's or spouse's child, grandchild, sibling or parent, plus the owner's uncle, aunt, nephew or niece.

  • File online, in person or by mail. Once granted, the application does not need repeating unless the assessor asks.
  • Each occupant, owner and spouse signs and supplies a Social Security number, so the state can confirm no other Minnesota homestead is claimed.
  • The driver's license must show the home address, because Minnesota requires an address change within 30 days.
  • A relative homestead does not qualify for the property tax refund. A property that was ever classified seasonal residential recreational under the current owner cannot take a relative homestead.

If you move out or stop qualifying, tell the assessor within 30 days. Miss that and the parcel can be recalculated as nonhomestead, with a penalty equal to 100 percent of the homestead benefit.

Call the assessor at 218-732-3552 first. After that, Minnesota Statutes 274.01 provides two stages. The local board of appeal and equalization, which is the town board or city council unless it has handed the job to the county, meets between April 1 and May 31 after at least ten days of published notice. It has 20 days from convening to finish, and its reductions cannot lower the assessor's total by more than one percent.

Skip the local board after being notified and you generally lose the right to appear at the county board, so the spring meeting is worth attending. A late disagreement goes to the county board of equalization, where the auditor serves. The last stop is Tax Court, and a district court petition for a given tax year is due April 30 of that year under Statutes 278.01.

• November 15: last day to pay the second half on qualifying agricultural property without penalty.
  • December: unpaid halves pick up another 1 percent each month until they reach the cap for the property type.
  • December 31, 2026: final day to apply for homestead on a home you owned and lived in during the year.
  • April 30, 2027: court filing date for a petition about taxes payable in 2027, which follows the March valuation notice.

If you close before December 31, mention the homestead deadline to the buyer. The buyer's own application is what carries the benefit into 2027 taxes, and the assessor at 218-732-3552 can mail or email the form.

sections.h2: Before you list a Hubbard County property
sections.html:
Start with the classification. Ask the assessor at 218-732-3552 whether the parcel is taxed as homestead, seasonal recreational or something else, because that one answer sets the penalty rates and the homestead rules a buyer will face. Next, find out which halves are paid. The Auditor/Treasurer can tell you whether anything is open from earlier years and whether the parcel appears on the published delinquent tax list.

Then plan the handoff. Give the buyer the date of the homestead deadline if your closing falls before it, and keep a copy of your latest statement for the title company. Doing these three things before a showing keeps the paperwork from slowing the sale later.

sections.h2: What a seller settles at closing
sections.html:
Delinquent tax gets paid before recording. Hubbard's recorder asks for this, and Minnesota Statutes 272.12 stops the auditor from transferring a parcel that still has delinquent tax on it. Current-year tax is not required at recording unless the parcel is being split, and it is usually collected through the closing settlement. Tax payments are not part of electronic recording, so your title company arranges the payoff separately.

The recorder takes abstract and Torrens documents through four trusted submitters: ePN, Indecomm Global Services, Corporation Service Company and Simplifile. State deed tax and mortgage registration tax are collected together with the recording fee. A deed uses an eCRV and, when needed, an electronic well disclosure certificate. For a current-year payoff figure, ask the Hubbard County Treasurer's Office, and ask the assessor how your lake home is classified, since that decides the penalty rates and homestead rules.

If the house is inherited, empty or behind on taxes, bring the parcel number and latest statement to the Auditor/Treasurer and ask what is owed through your expected closing date.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Hubbard County property tax?
faqs.a: At the Auditor/Treasurer in the Government Center in Park Rapids, or online through the Pay Your Taxes Online link on the county's I want to Pay page. Mailed payments need a postmark by the due date.

faqs.q: Does a Hubbard County cabin qualify for homestead?
faqs.a: Only if you own it and live there as your primary home, or a qualifying relative does. Seasonal residential recreational property is its own class, and a relative homestead is barred on any property that has carried that class under the current owner.

faqs.q: When must I apply for Hubbard County homestead?
faqs.a: By December 31, 2026 for the current assessment, which affects taxes payable in 2027. You must own and occupy the property by then, and you can apply online, in person or by mail.

faqs.q: Are Hubbard County property taxes paid at closing?
faqs.a: Often, yes, through the settlement statement, though current-year tax is not required at recording unless the parcel is split. Delinquent tax must be paid before the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: What is the Hubbard County assessor's phone number?
faqs.a: 218-732-3552, at Property Records, 301 Court Ave., Park Rapids, MN 56470. The same office handles valuation, classification, homestead and recording.
